The flu (influenza) is a viral infection that usually comes on quickly. Most people notice several symptoms at the same time. Common signs include:

• Fever – a higher than normal body temperature, often 100°F (38°C) or more  
• Chills – feeling cold and shivering even though you have a fever  
• Cough – usually dry (no mucus) at first, then it may become productive (producing mucus)  
• Sore throat – a scratchy or painful feeling in the throat when you swallow  
• Runny or stuffy nose – excess mucus that drips from the nose or makes it hard to breathe through the nostrils  
• Muscle aches – soreness in the arms, legs, back, or abdomen, often described as “body aches”  
• Headache – pressure or throbbing pain in the head  
• Fatigue – feeling unusually tired or weak, sometimes lasting for weeks after other symptoms improve  
• Sometimes you may have vomiting or diarrhea, especially in children

These symptoms usually start suddenly and can last about a week, though the feeling of tiredness can linger longer. If you have a very high fever, difficulty breathing, chest pain, sudden dizziness, or confusion, seek medical help right away, as these can be signs of a more serious illness.

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly, so the signs can be mild at first. Common symptoms include:

• Feeling very thirsty more often than usual – the body tries to replace fluid lost through extra urination.  
• Going to the bathroom a lot, especially at night – this is called polyuria, which means frequent urination.  
• Feeling unusually hungry even after eating – the body isn’t using sugar properly, so it signals for more food.  
• Unexplained weight loss – despite eating more, the body may break down fat and muscle for energy.  
• Feeling very tired or low on energy – cells aren’t getting enough sugar, the main fuel they need.  
• Blurred vision – high blood sugar can cause the eye’s lens to swell, making things look fuzzy.  
• Slow healing of cuts, bruises, or infections – high sugar levels can affect the body’s ability to repair tissue.  
• Numbness, tingling, or pain in the hands or feet – this is called peripheral neuropathy, a nerve problem caused by prolonged high blood sugar.

Sometimes people with type 2 diabetes have no noticeable symptoms at all, which is why regular screening is important, especially if you have risk factors such as being overweight, having a family history of diabetes, or being over age 45. If you notice any of these signs, talk to a health professional for testing and advice.

High blood pressure (also called hypertension) often does not cause any obvious signs, which is why it’s called a “silent” condition. Many people feel fine even when their pressure is too high. When symptoms do appear, they can include:

• Headaches, especially at the back of the head or in the morning  
• Dizziness or feeling light‑headed  
• Blurred or double vision  
• Shortness of breath, even with mild activity  
• Chest discomfort or a feeling of pressure in the chest  
• Fatigue or feeling unusually tired  
• Nosebleeds (these are less common and usually happen only when pressure is very high)  

Because most people with high blood pressure have no symptoms, the only reliable way to know if you have it is to have your blood pressure measured regularly by a health professional or with a home monitor. If you notice any of the above signs, especially if they come on suddenly or are severe, it’s a good idea to check your blood pressure and talk to a doctor.

Iron deficiency anemia happens when your body doesn’t have enough iron to make the red blood cells it needs. Without enough healthy red blood cells, you may notice several signs and symptoms. They can appear slowly and may be easy to miss at first.

Common symptoms include:

• Feeling unusually tired or weak – your body isn’t getting enough oxygen, so you get low energy.  
• Shortness of breath, especially during activities that used to be easy, like climbing stairs.  
• Pale skin, especially on the face, inside the lower eyelids, or on the nail beds.  
• Fast or irregular heartbeat – the heart works harder to move the limited oxygen around.  
• Dizziness or light‑headedness, sometimes feeling faint.  
• Cold hands and feet – reduced blood flow makes extremities feel chilly.  
• Headaches that happen more often than usual.  
• Cravings for non‑food items such as ice, dirt, or starch (a condition called pica).  
• Unusual cravings for or dislike of certain foods, especially meat.  
• Brittle nails that break easily or have a spoon‑shaped curve.  
• Restless legs syndrome – an uncomfortable urge to move the legs, especially at night.  

If you notice several of these signs, especially together, it’s a good idea to talk to a health professional. A simple blood test can confirm whether iron deficiency anemia is present, and treatment usually involves iron‑rich foods or supplements. Early detection helps prevent the symptoms from getting worse.

Asthma is a condition that makes the airways in the lungs become narrow and inflamed. When this happens, people often notice several signs that something is wrong with their breathing. Common symptoms include:

• Shortness of breath – feeling like you can’t get enough air, especially during activity or at night.  
• Wheezing – a high‑pitched whistling sound when you breathe out, caused by air moving through tightened airways.  
• Coughing – often a dry cough that may be worse at night, early in the morning, or after exercise.  
• Chest tightness – a feeling that something is squeezing or pressing on the chest.  

These symptoms can come and go. Some people have occasional flare‑ups, while others may have them more often. If you notice any of these signs, especially if they happen repeatedly or get worse, it’s a good idea to talk to a healthcare professional for evaluation and advice.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD, is when stomach acid frequently flows back up into the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach (the esophagus). This back‑flow can cause a range of signs that you might notice.

Common symptoms include:

• Heartburn – a burning feeling behind the breastbone that often gets worse after eating or when lying down.  
• Regurgitation – a sour or bitter taste in the mouth, or the sensation that food or liquid is coming back up.  
• Chest discomfort – pressure, tightness, or pain in the chest that can sometimes be mistaken for a heart problem.  
• Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) – feeling that food gets stuck or moves slowly down the throat.  
• Chronic cough – a cough that lasts for weeks without a clear reason, especially at night.  
• Hoarseness or sore throat – irritation from acid reaching the voice box.  
• Feeling of a lump in the throat (globus sensation) – a persistent sensation that something is stuck in the throat.  
• Bad breath – a sour or acidic smell caused by refluxed material.  

Less common signs that may appear, especially in children or older adults, are:

• Wheezing or asthma‑like symptoms.  
• Nausea or vomiting.  
• Weight loss if eating becomes uncomfortable.  

If you notice several of these symptoms, especially if they happen often or interfere with daily life, it’s a good idea to talk to a health professional for evaluation and possible treatment.

Strep throat is an infection of the throat caused by a type of bacteria called group A streptococcus. It can feel much worse than a regular sore throat. Common signs and symptoms include:

• Sudden, severe sore throat – the pain often comes on quickly and can make swallowing uncomfortable.  
• Painful swallowing – you may feel a sharp or burning sensation when you try to eat or drink.  
• Fever – a temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher is typical.  
• Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck – the small glands under the jaw may feel sore to the touch.  
• White or yellow spots on the tonsils or the back of the throat – these are patches of pus (dead white blood cells) that can be seen when you look in the mirror.  
• Redness of the throat and tonsils – the tissue may look bright red.  
• Headache – a dull or throbbing pain in the head is common.  
• Stomach upset, nausea, or vomiting – especially in children.  
• Loss of appetite – you might not feel like eating because swallowing hurts.  

These symptoms usually appear within two to five days after being exposed to the bacteria. Not every sore throat is strep; viral infections can cause similar signs but usually do not produce the white spots on the tonsils or the high fever that are more typical of strep throat. If you think you have strep, a doctor can do a quick throat swab test to confirm and prescribe antibiotics if needed.

Hepatitis C is an infection of the liver caused by a virus. Many people do not feel sick at first, but when symptoms do appear they can include:

• Feeling unusually tired or weak – the body is using extra energy to fight the infection.  
• Loss of appetite or nausea – you may not want to eat and might feel queasy.  
• Abdominal discomfort, especially in the upper right side where the liver sits.  
• Dark‑colored urine – the urine may look amber or brown because of extra waste products.  
• Pale‑colored stool – the stool can become lighter than normal.  
• Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes (jaundice) – this happens when the liver cannot process a pigment called bilirubin properly.  
• Joint or muscle aches – some people feel sore muscles or achy joints.  
• Fever or mild flu‑like feeling – a low‑grade fever can accompany the infection.  

In many cases, especially during the early (acute) stage, people have no noticeable signs at all. If the infection becomes chronic (lasting more than six months), symptoms may stay mild for years while the liver slowly gets damaged. When liver damage becomes more serious, additional signs can appear, such as swelling in the abdomen or legs, easy bruising or bleeding, and confusion or memory problems. If you notice any of these symptoms, especially jaundice or persistent fatigue, it’s a good idea to see a health professional for testing and advice.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed when blood‑sugar tests show levels that are higher than normal. Doctors usually use one of three main tests, and the results have to meet specific cut‑off numbers.

**Common tests**

• **Fasting plasma glucose (FPG)** – You fast (no food or drink except water) for at least 8 hours, then a blood sample is taken.  
 – A level of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher on two separate occasions means diabetes.  
 – Levels between 100 and 125 mg/dL are called “prediabetes,” a warning sign that diabetes could develop.

• **Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)** – After the same overnight fast, you drink a sugary liquid containing 75 g of glucose. Blood is drawn again after 2 hours.  
 – A 2‑hour level of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher on two separate tests confirms diabetes.  
 – Levels from 140 to 199 mg/dL indicate prediabetes.

• **Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c)** – This blood test measures the average blood‑sugar level over the past 2‑3 months.  
 – An A1c of 6.5 % or higher on two separate occasions means diabetes.  
 – An A1c between 5.7 % and 6.4 % is considered prediabetes.

**When a random (non‑fasting) test can be used**

If you have clear symptoms of high blood sugar—such as increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, or blurry vision—a single random blood‑glucose reading of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher can be enough for a diagnosis, without needing a fasting or A1c test.

**Screening recommendations**

• Adults aged 45 and older should be screened at least once, even if they have no symptoms.  
• Younger adults who are overweight, have a family history of diabetes, belong to a high‑risk ethnic group, or have conditions such as high blood pressure or high cholesterol should be screened earlier and more often.  
• If a test result falls in the prediabetes range, the doctor may repeat the test after a few months to confirm and discuss steps to prevent progression.

In practice, doctors often start with the A1c test because it does not require fasting. If the result is borderline, they may follow up with a fasting glucose or an oral glucose tolerance test to be certain. The goal is to catch the condition early so that lifestyle changes or medication can keep blood sugar under control and reduce the risk of complications.

High blood pressure, also called hypertension, is found by measuring the pressure of blood as it moves through the arteries. The diagnosis is made by a doctor or other health professional using a few simple steps.

• **Blood‑pressure reading** – A cuff is wrapped around the upper arm and inflated. As the cuff deflates, a machine records two numbers:  
  – **Systolic pressure** (the top number) shows the force when the heart squeezes and pushes blood out.  
  – **Diastolic pressure** (the bottom number) shows the force when the heart rests between beats.  

• **What counts as high** – In most guidelines, a reading of 130 mm Hg or higher for systolic, or 80 mm Hg or higher for diastolic, is considered high. “mm Hg” just means millimeters of mercury, the unit used for pressure.

• **Multiple measurements** – One single reading is not enough. The doctor will usually take at least two readings during the same visit, spaced a few minutes apart, and may ask you to come back for a second visit. This helps make sure the result is reliable and not affected by temporary factors like stress or caffeine.

• **Home or ambulatory monitoring** – If the office readings are borderline, the doctor may ask you to measure your blood pressure at home for a week, using a validated home cuff. Alternatively, a small device can be worn for 24 hours (ambulatory monitoring) to record pressure throughout daily activities and sleep. These methods give a fuller picture of your usual blood pressure.

• **Checking for other health issues** – While measuring pressure, the doctor may also look for signs of damage to the heart, kidneys, eyes, or blood vessels, because long‑term high pressure can affect these organs.

In short, high blood pressure is diagnosed when repeated, accurate measurements show the numbers are consistently at or above the defined thresholds. Regular check‑ups and, if needed, home or 24‑hour monitoring help confirm the diagnosis.

Pneumonia is usually found by a combination of talking with the patient, looking at the chest, and doing a few simple tests.

**1. Talk about symptoms**  
The doctor asks about things like cough, fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, and how long the symptoms have been present. This helps decide if pneumonia is likely.

**2. Physical exam**  
The doctor listens to the lungs with a stethoscope. In pneumonia, they often hear abnormal sounds called “crackles” or “rales,” which are like tiny popping noises that happen when air moves through fluid‑filled parts of the lungs.

**3. Chest X‑ray**  
A picture of the lungs taken from the front (and sometimes the side) shows areas that look white or cloudy. Those white spots are places where the lung tissue is filled with fluid or pus, which is typical for pneumonia.

**4. Laboratory tests**  
- **Blood test**: Checks for signs of infection, such as a higher white‑blood‑cell count.  
- **Sputum test**: The patient coughs up mucus (sputum) which is sent to a lab to see what germs might be causing the infection.  
- **Blood cultures**: If the fever is high, a sample of blood may be taken to see if the infection has spread into the bloodstream.

**5. Additional imaging (if needed)**  
- **CT scan**: A more detailed picture of the lungs, used when the X‑ray isn’t clear or if the doctor suspects complications.  
- **Ultrasound**: Sometimes used to look for fluid around the lungs (pleural effusion).

**6. Pulse oximetry**  
A small sensor placed on a fingertip measures how much oxygen is in the blood. Low oxygen levels can indicate that pneumonia is affecting breathing.

**7. Special tests for certain groups**  
- **Bronchoscopy**: A thin tube with a light is slipped down the throat to look directly at the airways and collect samples. This is usually reserved for people who are very sick or have underlying lung disease.  
- **Rapid antigen or PCR tests**: Quick tests that can detect specific viruses (like flu or COVID‑19) or bacteria from a nasal swab or sputum sample.

Putting all of these pieces together—symptoms, exam findings, imaging, and lab results—allows the doctor to confirm that pneumonia is present and to decide which treatment is best.

Anemia is found when a doctor looks at your symptoms, does a physical exam, and runs a few simple lab tests.

**What the doctor checks first**

• How you feel – tiredness, shortness of breath, pale skin, fast heartbeat, or feeling dizzy.  
• Physical signs – pale gums, nail beds, or the inside of the lower eyelids; a fast or irregular pulse; a heart murmur.

**Key laboratory test: the complete blood count (CBC)**  

The CBC is a single blood draw that gives several numbers:

• **Hemoglobin** – the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Low levels mean anemia.  
• **Hematocrit** – the percentage of your blood that is made up of red cells. A low percentage also points to anemia.  
• **Red‑cell count** – how many red blood cells are in a given volume of blood.  
• **Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)** – the average size of the red cells. This helps tell what type of anemia you might have (small, normal, or large cells).  
• **Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)** – how much hemoglobin each cell contains and how concentrated it is.

If any of these numbers are below the normal range, the doctor will look for the cause.

**Additional tests to find the cause**

• **Peripheral blood smear** – a tiny drop of blood is spread on a slide and looked at under a microscope. The shape and color of the cells can suggest iron deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, or other problems.  
• **Iron studies** – measure serum iron, ferritin (the body’s iron storage protein), total iron‑binding capacity, and sometimes transferrin saturation. Low iron or low ferritin usually means iron‑deficiency anemia.  
• **Vitamin B12 and folate levels** – low levels cause a type of anemia where the red cells are larger than normal.  
• **Reticulocyte count** – counts young red cells that the bone marrow is releasing. A high count means the marrow is trying hard to replace lost cells; a low count means the marrow isn’t making enough.  
• **Kidney function tests** – the kidneys make a hormone (erythropoietin) that tells the marrow to make red cells. Poor kidney function can lead to anemia.  
• **Stool occult blood test** – checks for hidden blood in the stool, which can point to bleeding in the gastrointestinal tract as a source of iron loss.  
• **Other specific tests** – depending on clues, the doctor may order tests for chronic disease, autoimmune disorders, or genetic conditions (such as sickle‑cell disease or thalassemia).

**Putting it all together**

The doctor combines the symptom check, physical exam, CBC numbers, and any follow‑up tests to confirm that anemia is present and to figure out why it is happening. Once the cause is known, treatment can be directed at that specific problem.

Hypothyroidism is diagnosed by combining what a person feels, what a doctor finds on exam, and a few simple blood tests.

**What the doctor looks for**

• Symptoms such as feeling unusually tired, gaining weight, feeling cold, dry skin, hair loss, constipation, or having a slow heartbeat.  
• A physical exam may show a swollen neck (enlarged thyroid gland), dry skin, or a slower reflex response.

**Blood tests**

The most important tests measure the hormones that the thyroid makes and the signal that tells the thyroid to work.

• **TSH (thyroid‑stimulating hormone)** – This is a chemical made by the pituitary gland that tells the thyroid to produce its hormones. In hypothyroidism the pituitary makes more TSH, so the level is high.  
• **Free T4 (free thyroxine)** – This is the main hormone the thyroid releases. In hypothyroidism the amount of free T4 is low.  
• Sometimes doctors also check **free T3** (another thyroid hormone) and **thyroid antibodies** (proteins that show if the immune system is attacking the thyroid, which is common in an autoimmune form called Hashimoto’s disease).

**How the results are used**

• A high TSH together with a low free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism (the problem is in the thyroid itself).  
• If TSH is high but free T4 is still normal, the condition is called subclinical hypothyroidism; doctors may monitor it or start treatment depending on symptoms and other risk factors.  
• If both TSH and free T4 are low, the problem may be in the pituitary gland rather than the thyroid (secondary hypothyroidism), and further testing is needed.

**Additional checks (when needed)**

• An ultrasound of the neck can look at the size and texture of the thyroid if a lump or enlargement is felt.  
• A radioactive iodine uptake scan may be ordered if the doctor wants to see how well the thyroid is taking up iodine, but this is rarely needed for routine diagnosis.

**Who gets screened**

• Women over age 60, people with a family history of thyroid disease, those who have had neck radiation, or people with autoimmune disorders are often screened with a simple TSH blood test even if they have no symptoms.

In short, diagnosing hypothyroidism starts with noticing the signs, confirming them with a high TSH and low free T4 blood test, and then adding any extra tests if the picture is unclear.

Hepatitis B is diagnosed mainly by looking at blood samples and checking how the liver is working. The process usually follows these steps:

• **Screening blood test** – A simple blood draw is taken to look for specific proteins and antibodies that the virus or the body’s immune response makes.  
 - **HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen)** – If this protein is present, it means the virus is currently in the body.  
 - **Anti‑HBs (antibody to the surface antigen)** – This antibody shows up after a person has cleared the infection or after successful vaccination.  
 - **Anti‑HBc (antibody to the core antigen)** – This appears when the immune system has reacted to the inner part of the virus; it can be present during an active infection or after it has resolved.  
 - **HBV‑DNA** – A test that measures the amount of viral genetic material (DNA) in the blood; it tells how much virus is replicating.

• **Liver function tests** – Blood tests that check enzymes such as ALT and AST. High levels suggest the liver is inflamed or damaged, which often happens with hepatitis B.

• **Additional blood work if needed** – Tests for other viruses (like hepatitis C), for HIV, or for markers of liver disease (e.g., bilirubin, albumin) may be ordered to get a full picture.

• **Imaging studies** – An ultrasound or other imaging scan can look at the liver’s size and shape and check for signs of scarring (cirrhosis) or tumors.

• **Liver biopsy (rarely needed)** – A tiny piece of liver tissue is taken with a needle and examined under a microscope. This is done only when doctors need detailed information about the amount of scarring or inflammation.

**Who gets tested?**  
People at higher risk are often screened, such as:

• Those born in countries where hepatitis B is common.  
• People who have had unprotected sex with multiple partners.  
• Individuals who use injection drugs.  
• Healthcare workers who might be exposed to blood.  
• Anyone who has a close family member with chronic hepatitis B.  
• Pregnant women, because the virus can be passed to the baby.

**What the results mean**

- If HBsAg is positive and anti‑HBs is negative, the infection is active.  
- If both HBsAg and anti‑HBs are negative but anti‑HBc is positive, the person had a past infection that has cleared.  
- If only anti‑HBs is positive, the person is immune, usually because of vaccination.  
- The level of HBV‑DNA helps doctors decide how aggressive treatment should be.

By combining these blood tests with liver enzyme results, imaging, and sometimes a biopsy, doctors can confirm whether someone has hepatitis B, tell if the infection is new or long‑standing, and decide the best plan for monitoring or treatment.

The flu (influenza) is a viral infection that usually gets better on its own, but treatment focuses on easing symptoms, staying hydrated, and preventing complications.

**Rest and fluids**  
• Get plenty of sleep and take it easy while your body fights the virus.  
• Drink water, clear soups, herbal tea, or electrolyte drinks often. Staying hydrated helps loosen mucus and keeps you from getting dehydrated.

**Medication for symptoms**  
• Over‑the‑counter pain relievers such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen can lower fever, relieve aches, and reduce headache.  
• Cough suppressants or expectorants can help if you have a bothersome cough, but they are not required for recovery.  
• Decongestant tablets or nasal sprays may ease a blocked nose, but they should be used only for a short time.

**Antiviral medicines**  
• Prescription antivirals (for example, oseltamivir, zanamivir, or baloxavir) can shorten the illness by about a day if started within 48 hours of symptom onset.  
• These drugs are most useful for people at higher risk of complications, such as older adults, young children, pregnant women, or anyone with chronic heart, lung, or immune‑system problems.

**When to see a health professional**  
• If you have difficulty breathing, chest pain, persistent high fever, severe vomiting, or confusion.  
• If symptoms improve for a few days and then suddenly get worse, which can signal a secondary bacterial infection like pneumonia.  
• If you belong to a high‑risk group and your symptoms are not improving after a couple of days.

**Home care tips**  
• Use a humidifier or sit in a steamy bathroom to keep air moist, which can soothe a sore throat and ease breathing.  
• Gargle with warm salt water to reduce throat irritation.  
• Keep your hands clean and avoid close contact with others to prevent spreading the virus.

Most healthy people recover from the flu within one to two weeks with these supportive measures. If you have any doubts or your condition worsens, contact a medical professional promptly.

Type 2 diabetes is managed with a combination of everyday habits, medicines and regular check‑ups. The goal is to keep blood‑sugar levels in a safe range so the body works well and complications are avoided.

**Lifestyle changes**  
These are the first steps and often make the biggest difference.

• Eat a balanced diet – choose plenty of vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins and healthy fats. Limit sugary drinks, sweets and refined carbs (like white bread).  
• Control portion sizes – eating smaller meals more often can help keep blood sugar steady.  
• Stay active – aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week (for example brisk walking, cycling, swimming). Exercise helps the body use insulin more efficiently.  
• Lose excess weight – even a modest loss of 5‑10 % of body weight can improve blood‑sugar control.  
• Quit smoking and limit alcohol – both can affect blood sugar and heart health.

**Blood‑sugar monitoring**  
Checking blood glucose (the amount of sugar in the blood) tells you how well your plan is working.

• Home glucose meters let you test a finger‑stick sample several times a day.  
• Your doctor may also order a lab test called HbA1c, which shows average blood sugar over the past 2‑3 months.

**Medications**  
If lifestyle changes are not enough, medicines are added. They work in different ways:

• Metformin – the most common first‑line drug; it reduces the liver’s production of glucose and improves the body’s response to insulin.  
• Sulfonylureas – stimulate the pancreas to release more insulin.  
• GLP‑1 receptor agonists – mimic a natural hormone that increases insulin release, slows digestion and can help with weight loss.  
• SGLT2 inhibitors – cause the kidneys to excrete extra glucose in the urine, also offering heart and kidney benefits.  
• DPP‑4 inhibitors – keep another natural hormone active longer, helping the pancreas release insulin when needed.  
• Insulin therapy – sometimes needed if other medicines are not enough; it replaces or adds to the insulin the body makes.

Your doctor will choose the medication(s) that fit your health situation, other conditions, and preferences.

**Other treatments**  

• Bariatric (weight‑loss) surgery – for people with severe obesity, surgery can dramatically improve blood‑sugar control and may even put diabetes into remission.  
• Regular eye, foot and kidney checks – diabetes can affect these organs, so routine exams help catch problems early.

**Putting it all together**  

1. Follow a healthy eating plan and stay active.  
2. Monitor blood sugar as advised.  
3. Take prescribed medicines exactly as directed.  
4. Attend regular medical appointments for labs and screenings.  
5. Adjust the plan with your health‑care team if anything changes.

By combining these steps, most people with type 2 diabetes can keep their blood sugar in a safe range and lead active, healthy lives.

A urinary tract infection (UTI) is usually treated with medicines and simple home care. The goal is to clear the infection, relieve symptoms, and prevent it from coming back.

**Antibiotics**  
The main treatment is a short course of antibiotics, which are medicines that kill the bacteria causing the infection.  
• Your doctor will choose the specific antibiotic based on the type of bacteria and any recent antibiotic use.  
• Most people take the medicine for 3 to 7 days; a longer course may be needed for more serious infections.  
• It’s important to finish the whole prescription, even if you feel better before the pills are gone, to make sure all the bacteria are gone.

**Hydration**  
Drinking plenty of fluids helps flush bacteria out of the urinary system.  
• Aim for at least 8 glasses (about 2 liters) of water a day, unless your doctor tells you otherwise.  
• Cranberry juice or unsweetened cranberry drinks are sometimes suggested, but they are not a substitute for antibiotics.

**Pain and symptom relief**  
If you have burning, urgency, or lower‑abdominal pain, over‑the‑counter medicines can help.  
• Acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) can reduce pain and fever.  
• Some doctors may prescribe a medication called phenazopyridine for a few days to ease urinary burning; it only masks symptoms, so it’s used together with antibiotics.

**Follow‑up**  
• Most uncomplicated UTIs improve within a couple of days. If symptoms persist after finishing antibiotics, call your doctor.  
• In some cases, a urine test may be repeated to make sure the infection is completely gone, especially for pregnant women or people with kidney problems.

**Preventing future infections**  
• Urinate soon after sex to help clear any bacteria that may have entered the urethra.  
• Wipe from front to back after using the toilet to keep bacteria from the anal area away from the urinary opening.  
• Stay well‑hydrated and empty your bladder regularly; don’t hold urine for long periods.  
• Avoid irritating feminine products such as douches, powders, or scented soaps in the genital area.

If you think you have a UTI, see a healthcare provider for a urine test and appropriate antibiotic prescription. Prompt treatment usually clears the infection quickly and reduces the chance of complications.

Asthma is a condition where the airways in the lungs become tight and inflamed, making it hard to breathe. Treatment focuses on two goals: stopping attacks quickly when they happen and keeping the lungs calm so attacks are less likely.

**Quick‑relief (rescue) medicines**  
These are used at the first sign of an asthma flare‑up to open the airways right away.

• Short‑acting bronchodilator inhaler – a small puff that relaxes the muscles around the airway, letting air flow in more easily.  
• Nebulizer treatment – a machine that turns liquid medicine into a fine mist you breathe in, useful for young children or during a severe attack.  

**Long‑term control medicines**  
These are taken every day to reduce inflammation and keep the airways from tightening in the first place.

• Inhaled corticosteroid – a low‑dose steroid spray that lowers swelling inside the lungs.  
• Long‑acting bronchodilator – a medicine that keeps the airway muscles relaxed for many hours; often combined with an inhaled steroid in one inhaler.  
• Leukotriene modifier – a pill that blocks chemicals that cause airway narrowing and swelling.  
• Biologic therapy – an injection for people with severe asthma; it targets specific parts of the immune system that trigger attacks.  

**Avoiding triggers**  
Many things can set off asthma, so reducing exposure helps control the disease.

• Smoke (cigarettes, wood fire, etc.)  
• Dust mites and pet dander  
• Pollen, mold, or strong odors  
• Cold air or sudden exercise without a warm‑up  

**Lifestyle and self‑care steps**

• Use a peak‑flow meter – a small device that measures how fast you can blow air out; it helps you see early changes in lung function.  
• Follow an asthma action plan – a written guide from your doctor that tells you what medicines to take at each symptom level.  
• Warm up before exercise and consider using a quick‑relief inhaler right before activity if exercise triggers symptoms.  
• Keep your inhaler clean and check the expiration date regularly.  

**Regular check‑ups**  
Seeing a healthcare provider every few months lets the doctor adjust medicines, review your action plan, and make sure your asthma stays well‑controlled.

By combining quick‑relief inhalers for emergencies, daily medicines to keep inflammation low, and steps to avoid known triggers, most people with asthma can live active, comfortable lives. If symptoms worsen or you need your rescue inhaler more often than usual, contact a medical professional promptly.

Gastro‑esophageal reflux disease (GERD) is when stomach acid frequently flows back into the tube that carries food to the stomach (the esophagus). This can cause heartburn, chest discomfort, and other symptoms. Treatment aims to reduce the amount of acid that comes up and to heal any irritation.

**Lifestyle and diet changes**  
• Eat smaller meals and avoid large, heavy dinners.  
• Don’t lie down for at least two to three hours after eating.  
• Raise the head of the bed about 6‑10 cm (a wedge pillow works too) to keep acid down while you sleep.  
• Limit foods and drinks that relax the lower esophageal sphincter (the valve that keeps stomach contents from coming up). Common triggers are:  
 – Chocolate  
 – Caffeine (coffee, tea, soda)  
 – Alcohol  
 – Spicy or fried foods  
 – Citrus fruits and tomato‑based sauces  
• Quit smoking; nicotine can weaken the valve.  
• Maintain a healthy weight—extra belly fat can push the stomach upward and increase reflux.

**Medications**  
• Antacids (e.g., calcium carbonate) – neutralize acid quickly for occasional heartburn.  
• H2‑blockers (e.g., ranitidine, famotidine) – lower acid production for a longer period than antacids.  
• Proton‑pump inhibitors (PPIs) (e.g., omeprazole, lansoprazole) – the strongest acid‑reducing drugs; they allow the esophagus to heal and are often used for daily, long‑term control.  
• Prokinetics (e.g., metoclopramide) – help the stomach empty faster, reducing the chance of reflux; used less often because of side‑effects.

**When medication isn’t enough**  
If symptoms persist despite lifestyle changes and medicines, a doctor may suggest procedures to strengthen the valve or repair damage.

• Endoscopic therapies – a thin tube with a camera is used to apply heat, radio‑frequency energy, or small stitches to tighten the valve.  
• Surgical fundoplication – the upper part of the stomach is wrapped around the lower esophagus to reinforce the valve. This can be done laparoscopically (through small incisions).  
• Magnetic sphincter augmentation – a ring of tiny magnetic beads is placed around the lower esophagus; the magnets help keep the valve closed but still allow food to pass.

**Follow‑up care**  
Regular check‑ups help ensure the treatment is working and that any complications, such as inflammation or narrowing of the esophagus, are caught early.

In most people, a combination of diet changes, weight control, and medication provides good relief. Surgery or endoscopic procedures are reserved for those whose symptoms stay severe despite those measures.

Iron deficiency anemia is treated by getting more iron into the body and fixing anything that is causing the loss of iron. The main steps are:

• **Increase iron in the diet** – eat foods that are rich in iron such as red meat, poultry, fish, beans, lentils, tofu, fortified cereals, spinach, and other dark‑green leafy vegetables.  

• **Take iron supplements** – most people are given a pill that contains iron (often ferrous sulfate, ferrous gluconate, or ferrous fumarate). The pill is usually taken on an empty stomach for best absorption, but if it upsets the stomach it can be taken with a small amount of food.  

• **Add vitamin C** – vitamin C (found in citrus fruits, strawberries, bell peppers, etc.) helps the body absorb iron better, so a glass of orange juice or a vitamin C tablet taken with the iron pill can be useful.  

• **Avoid things that block iron absorption** – coffee, tea, dairy products, and some whole‑grain foods contain substances that can make iron harder to absorb. It’s best to keep these away from the iron pill for a couple of hours.  

• **Treat the underlying cause** – if the anemia is due to bleeding (for example from heavy periods, a stomach ulcer, or a parasite infection), that source of blood loss must be stopped or treated.  

• **Intravenous (IV) iron** – when oral pills don’t work well, cause severe side effects, or when a rapid increase in iron is needed (such as before surgery), iron can be given through a vein in a clinic or hospital.  

• **Follow‑up testing** – doctors usually check blood tests after a few weeks and again after a few months to see if hemoglobin and iron stores are improving. The treatment is continued for several months after the blood numbers look normal to refill the body’s iron reserves.  

**What to expect while taking iron pills**

- Common side effects are stomach upset, constipation, or dark stools. Drinking plenty of water, eating a small amount of food, or switching to a different iron formulation can help.
- If you notice severe stomach pain, vomiting, or an allergic reaction (rash, swelling, trouble breathing), seek medical help right away.

By combining a diet rich in iron, taking supplements as directed, correcting any sources of blood loss, and monitoring progress with a doctor, most people recover fully from iron deficiency anemia.

Eczema, also called atopic dermatitis, is a skin condition that makes the skin red, itchy, and sometimes cracked or weepy. Treatment focuses on calming the inflammation, keeping the skin moisturized, and avoiding things that make it flare up.

**Basic skin‑care steps**

• **Moisturize often** – Use a thick, fragrance‑free cream or ointment (often called an “emollient”) at least twice a day and right after a bath. This helps repair the skin’s barrier and reduces dryness.  
• **Gentle cleansing** – Wash with lukewarm water and a mild, fragrance‑free cleanser. Avoid hot water and harsh soaps, which can strip natural oils.  
• **Short, lukewarm baths** – Adding a small amount of colloidal oatmeal or a prescribed bath oil can soothe itching. Pat the skin dry and apply moisturizer while the skin is still slightly damp.

**Medication options**

• **Topical steroids** – Creams or ointments that contain a mild to moderate strength steroid (for example, hydrocortisone 1% or a prescription strength) reduce redness and itching. Use them only on the affected areas for the short time your doctor advises, because long‑term use can thin the skin.  
• **Topical calcineurin inhibitors** – Products such as tacrolimus or pimecrolimus work by calming the immune response in the skin without the thinning effect of steroids. They are useful for sensitive areas like the face or folds.  
• **Antihistamines** – Oral antihistamines (often the non‑sedating kind) can help control itching, especially at night, making it easier to sleep. They do not treat the skin inflammation directly.  
• **Wet‑wrap therapy** – After applying a steroid or moisturizer, a damp layer of clothing or gauze is placed over the skin, then covered with a dry layer. This helps the medication soak in and hydrates the skin. It is usually done for a few hours under a doctor’s guidance.  
• **Phototherapy** – Controlled exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light in a medical setting can calm severe eczema that does not respond to creams. The doctor monitors the dose to avoid skin damage.  
• **Systemic medications** – For very severe or widespread eczema, doctors may prescribe oral steroids, a drug called methotrexate, or newer biologic medicines such as dupilumab. These work throughout the whole body and are used only when other treatments have not helped.

**Lifestyle and trigger‑avoidance tips**

• Identify and avoid personal triggers, which may include certain soaps, detergents, wool clothing, dust mites, pet dander, or specific foods.  
• Keep nails short and smooth to reduce skin damage from scratching.  
• Use a humidifier in dry indoor environments to add moisture to the air.  
• Wear soft, breathable fabrics like cotton; avoid rough or tight clothing that can irritate the skin.  
• Manage stress through relaxation techniques, as stress can worsen eczema for many people.

**When to see a doctor**

• If the rash spreads, becomes painful, oozes, or shows signs of infection such as increased warmth, swelling, or yellow crusts.  
• If over‑the‑counter moisturizers and mild steroids do not improve symptoms after a couple of weeks.  
• If you need help identifying triggers or creating a long‑term treatment plan.

By combining regular moisturization, appropriate medications, and avoidance of known irritants, most people can keep eczema under control and reduce flare‑ups. If you’re unsure which approach is right for you, talk with a dermatologist or primary‑care provider for a personalized plan.

Hypothyroidism means the thyroid gland is not making enough thyroid hormone. The goal of treatment is to replace the missing hormone so the body can work normally.

**Main treatment**

• **Synthetic thyroid hormone (levothyroxine)** – This is a man‑made version of the hormone thyroxine (T4) that the thyroid normally makes. It is taken as a pill once a day, usually in the morning on an empty stomach. The dose is set by the doctor based on your age, weight, other health problems and the results of blood tests.

**How the dose is decided**

• The doctor starts with a low dose and checks blood levels of thyroid hormone after a few weeks.  
• If the level is still low, the dose is increased a little.  
• This step‑by‑step approach continues until the blood test shows a normal level and you feel better.

**Things to remember while taking the medicine**

• Take the pill with a full glass of water and wait at least 30 minutes before eating or drinking anything else.  
• Certain foods and supplements (like soy, high‑fiber foods, calcium or iron tablets) can make the medicine work less well, so keep a consistent routine.  
• If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it’s almost time for the next one; then just skip the missed dose and continue as usual.

**Monitoring**

• Blood tests are done every 6–8 weeks after a dose change, then usually once a year once the dose is stable.  
• The doctor looks at two main numbers: TSH (thyroid‑stimulating hormone) and free T4. A normal TSH means the dose is right.

**Other possible treatments**

• In rare cases where levothyroxine cannot be used (for example, allergy or certain stomach problems), a combination of T4 and T3 (another thyroid hormone) may be prescribed.  
• If the thyroid is still present but not working, some doctors may give a small amount of natural thyroid extract, but this is less common.

**Lifestyle tips that help**

• Eat a balanced diet with enough iodine (found in dairy, fish, iodized salt) because iodine is needed to make thyroid hormone, but most people get enough from food.  
• Regular exercise and good sleep support overall metabolism and can make you feel better as the hormone level normalizes.  
• Keep a list of any new symptoms and share them with your doctor; sometimes the dose needs fine‑tuning.

In short, most people with hypothyroidism feel well by taking a daily pill of synthetic thyroid hormone, checking blood levels regularly, and following a consistent routine. If you have any concerns or side effects, talk to your healthcare provider.

Preventing the flu (influenza) is mostly about keeping the virus from getting into your body and helping your immune system stay strong. Here are the most effective steps you can take:

• Get the flu vaccine each year.  
  The shot trains your immune system to recognize the virus, so if you are exposed you are much less likely to get sick or you will have milder symptoms.

• Wash your hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds.  
  If soap isn’t available, use an alcohol‑based hand sanitizer. Clean hands remove the virus that may be on surfaces.

• Avoid touching your face, especially your eyes, nose, and mouth.  
  The virus can enter your body through these openings.

• Keep a safe distance from people who are coughing or sneezing.  
  Flu spreads through tiny droplets that travel when an infected person talks, coughs, or sneezes.

• Cover your coughs and sneezes with a tissue or the inside of your elbow.  
  This stops droplets from spreading into the air.

• Clean and disinfect frequently touched objects daily.  
  Handles, phones, keyboards, and light switches can hold the virus for several hours.

• Stay healthy with good habits:  
  – Eat a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.  
  – Get enough sleep (7‑9 hours for most adults).  
  – Stay physically active; regular exercise supports immune function.  
  – Manage stress, because chronic stress can weaken your defenses.

• If you feel sick, stay home and limit contact with others.  
  Staying isolated while you have symptoms reduces the chance of passing the virus to family, friends, or coworkers.

• Consider antiviral medication if you are at high risk (for example, older adults, pregnant people, or those with chronic health conditions) and have been exposed to the flu.  
  A doctor can prescribe pills that can prevent the virus from taking hold if started early.

By combining vaccination with good hygiene, healthy lifestyle choices, and staying home when ill, you greatly lower your chances of catching or spreading the flu.

Preventing type 2 diabetes mainly means keeping your blood sugar and weight in a healthy range. The good news is that most of the steps you can take are simple lifestyle habits that also improve overall health.

• Maintain a healthy weight  
  • Even a modest loss of 5‑10 % of body weight can lower your risk.  
  • Focus on steady, realistic changes rather than crash diets.

• Eat a balanced, fiber‑rich diet  
  • Choose whole grains, beans, fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds.  
  • Limit sugary drinks, sweets, and refined carbs (like white bread and pastries).  
  • Include a source of protein (lean meat, fish, tofu, legumes) at each meal to help control hunger.

• Control portion sizes  
  • Use smaller plates or measure servings to avoid overeating.  
  • Pay attention to hunger cues and stop eating when you feel satisfied, not stuffed.

• Stay physically active  
  • Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week (for example, brisk walking, cycling, swimming).  
  • Break it into 30‑minute sessions on most days, or shorter bouts that add up.  
  • Add strength‑training exercises (like lifting light weights or using resistance bands) twice a week to build muscle, which helps the body use sugar better.

• Limit sedentary time  
  • If you work at a desk, stand up and move for a few minutes every hour.  
  • Replace some TV or screen time with light activity, such as a short walk.

• Avoid smoking and limit alcohol  
  • Smoking raises insulin resistance, making blood sugar harder to control.  
  • If you drink alcohol, keep it moderate (up to one drink per day for women, up to two for men) and avoid sugary mixers.

• Get enough sleep  
  • Aim for 7‑9 hours of quality sleep each night.  
  • Poor sleep can affect hormones that control appetite and blood sugar.

• Manage stress  
  • Chronic stress can raise blood‑sugar levels.  
  • Try relaxation techniques such as deep breathing, meditation, yoga, or simple hobbies you enjoy.

• Regular health check‑ups  
  • If you have risk factors (family history, overweight, high blood pressure, or a history of gestational diabetes), ask your doctor to test your blood sugar periodically.  
  • Early detection allows you to act before diabetes develops.

By combining these habits—healthy eating, regular movement, weight control, and good sleep—you can significantly lower the chance of developing type 2 diabetes. Small, consistent changes are more sustainable than drastic, short‑term fixes.

Kidney stones are hard, crystal‑like deposits that can form in the kidneys and cause pain when they move.  Most stones can be helped or prevented by simple lifestyle changes.

**Drink plenty of fluids**  
• Aim for about 2 to 3 liters (about 8‑12 cups) of water each day.  
• A clear or light‑yellow urine color shows you’re drinking enough.  
• If you exercise, live in a hot climate, or sweat a lot, increase your fluid intake.

**Watch what you eat**  

*Calcium*  
• Getting enough calcium from foods such as milk, yogurt, cheese, leafy greens, and fortified plant milks can actually lower the risk of stones.  
• Avoid taking large calcium supplements without a doctor’s advice, because too much calcium from pills can raise stone risk.

*Oxalate* (a natural substance that can bind with calcium to form stones)  
• Foods high in oxalate include spinach, rhubarb, beets, nuts, chocolate, and tea.  
• You don’t have to stop them completely, but try to keep portions moderate and pair them with calcium‑rich foods, which can keep oxalate from being absorbed.

*Salt (sodium)*  
• Too much salt makes the kidneys excrete more calcium, which can help stones form.  
• Limit processed foods, canned soups, salty snacks, and add only a small pinch of salt to meals.

*Animal protein* (meat, fish, eggs, dairy)  
• High‑protein diets can increase the amount of acid in urine, encouraging certain stones.  
• Aim for a balanced amount—about 0.8‑1 gram of protein per kilogram of body weight per day—and include plant‑based proteins like beans and lentils.

*Sugar and sugary drinks*  
• Regular soda and sweetened drinks raise the risk of stones, especially those made from fructose.  
• Choose water, herbal tea, or plain milk instead.

**Maintain a healthy weight**  
• Being overweight can change the chemistry of urine and raise stone risk.  
• Regular physical activity and a balanced diet help keep weight in a healthy range.

**Consider your medical history**  
• If you’ve had stones before, your doctor may test your urine and blood to see which type you’re prone to.  
• Some people need specific medicines (for example, thiazide diuretics for calcium stones or allopurinol for uric‑acid stones).  
• Talk to a healthcare provider before starting any medication.

**Other practical tips**  

• Spread fluid intake throughout the day; sipping water regularly is better than drinking a large amount all at once.  
• If you find plain water boring, add a splash of lemon or lime for flavor—citrus can help prevent certain stones.  
• Avoid excessive vitamin C supplements (more than 1,000 mg per day) because the body can turn extra vitamin C into oxalate.  
• If you have a history of gout (high uric acid), controlling uric acid levels with diet and medication can lower the chance of uric‑acid stones.

**When to see a doctor**  
• If you’ve had a kidney stone, get a follow‑up test to find out its type.  
• If you notice blood in the urine, severe pain, or frequent urinary infections, seek medical attention promptly.

By staying well‑hydrated, eating a balanced diet with moderate calcium, low salt, and reasonable amounts of oxalate‑rich foods, keeping a healthy weight, and following any doctor‑recommended treatments, you can greatly reduce the chance of kidney stones forming.

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) happen when bacteria get into the bladder or urethra and start to grow. Keeping the urinary system clean and helping it flush out bacteria are the main ways to lower the risk.

**Everyday habits that help prevent UTIs**

• **Drink plenty of fluids** – Aim for at least 6‑8 glasses of water a day. More fluid means you urinate more often, which washes bacteria out of the bladder.

• **Empty your bladder regularly** – Don’t hold urine for long periods. Go when you feel the urge, especially after sex.

• **Wipe front‑to‑back** – After using the toilet, wipe from the front (the urethra) toward the back (the anus). This prevents bacteria from the bowel from moving toward the urinary opening.

• **Urinate after sexual activity** – A quick bathroom visit after sex helps flush any bacteria that may have been pushed toward the urethra.

• **Choose breathable underwear** – Cotton underwear and loose‑fitting clothes keep the area dry. Moisture encourages bacterial growth.

• **Avoid irritating products** – Stay away from scented soaps, bubble baths, douches, and feminine sprays in the genital area. These can irritate the urethra and make it easier for bacteria to stick.

• **Stay hydrated during illness** – If you have a fever or are vomiting, keep drinking fluids so your urine stays dilute and the bladder continues to empty well.

• **Consider probiotic foods** – Yogurt, kefir, and other foods with live cultures can support healthy bacteria in the gut, which may reduce the chance of harmful bacteria spreading to the urinary tract.

• **Cranberry products may help** – Some studies suggest unsweetened cranberry juice or capsules can make it harder for bacteria to attach to the bladder wall, but they are not a cure. Use them as part of a broader prevention plan.

**When to see a doctor**

If you notice any of these signs, get medical advice promptly:

- Burning or pain when you pee
- Frequent urge to urinate but only a little comes out
- Cloudy, dark, or foul‑smelling urine
- Blood in the urine
- Pain in the lower abdomen or back

Early treatment can stop an infection from spreading to the kidneys, which can be more serious.

By keeping the urinary system flushed, staying dry, and avoiding irritants, you can greatly lower the chance of getting a urinary tract infection.

Hepatitis B is a virus that can damage the liver. The good news is that there are several ways to keep it from spreading.

• Get the hepatitis B vaccine.  
   The vaccine is given as a series of three shots and creates protection that lasts for many years. It is safe for babies, children, teens and adults.

• Practice safe sex.  
   Use a condom every time you have vaginal, anal or oral sex. Condoms help stop the virus from moving from one partner to another.

• Don’t share needles or other drug‑using equipment.  
   If you inject drugs, use a clean needle each time. Many community programs give out sterile needles to help prevent infection.

• Make sure blood products are screened.  
   In most countries, blood donated for transfusions is tested for hepatitis B, so receiving screened blood is safe.

• Be careful with personal items that might have blood on them.  
   Avoid sharing razors, toothbrushes, or anything that could have tiny amounts of blood.

• Prevent mother‑to‑baby transmission.  
   Pregnant women are tested for hepatitis B. If a mother is infected, the baby receives the hepatitis B vaccine and a dose of hepatitis B immune globulin (a short‑term protection) within 12 hours of birth. This greatly reduces the chance the baby will become infected.

• Follow good hygiene in health‑care settings.  
   Health workers use gloves, masks and proper cleaning of equipment to keep the virus from spreading.

By combining vaccination with these everyday safety steps, the risk of getting hepatitis B can be kept very low.

Skin cancer is the most common type of cancer, but many cases can be avoided by protecting your skin from the sun’s harmful rays and checking your skin regularly.

**Everyday steps to lower your risk**

• **Use sunscreen** – Choose a sunscreen that blocks both UVA and UVB rays (look for “broad‑spectrum”) with a sun‑protection factor (SPF) of 30 or higher. Apply it generously to all exposed skin about 15 minutes before going outside, and reapply every two hours, or sooner if you’re swimming or sweating.

• **Wear protective clothing** – Long‑sleeved shirts, pants, wide‑brimmed hats, and sunglasses that block UV light help keep the sun off your skin. Some clothing is made with special fabrics that have a built‑in UV rating (called UPF).

• **Seek shade** – When the sun is strongest, usually between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., stay in the shade as much as possible. If you’re outdoors, bring an umbrella, a pop‑up canopy, or sit under a tree.

• **Avoid tanning beds** – The artificial UV light from tanning beds can damage skin just like the sun and greatly increases the chance of skin cancer.

• **Check your skin regularly** – Look at your whole body once a month for any new spots, or changes in existing moles. Use the “ABCDE” guide to spot worrisome features:
  - **A**symmetry – one half of the spot doesn’t match the other.
  - **B**order – edges are irregular, ragged, or blurred.
  - **C**olor – more than one shade, especially dark or uneven.
  - **D**iameter – larger than about the size of a pencil eraser (6 mm).
  - **E**volving – any change in size, shape, color, or feeling.

• **See a doctor promptly** – If you notice any of the ABCDE signs, a new growth, or a sore that doesn’t heal, schedule an appointment with a dermatologist (a skin doctor). Early detection makes treatment much easier.

**Lifestyle habits that help**

• **Eat a balanced diet** rich in fruits, vegetables, and foods containing antioxidants (like vitamins C and E). These nutrients help protect skin cells from damage.

• **Stay hydrated** – Drinking enough water keeps skin healthy and may improve its ability to repair minor damage.

• **Limit alcohol** – Heavy drinking can weaken the immune system, making it harder for the body to fight off abnormal skin cells.

By combining sun protection, regular skin checks, and healthy habits, you can greatly lower your chances of developing skin cancer. If you have a personal or family history of skin cancer, talk with your doctor about a more tailored prevention plan.

Hypertension, often called high blood pressure, is a condition where the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries is consistently too high.  

Why it matters  
• When the pressure stays high, the heart has to work harder to pump blood.  
• Over time this can damage blood vessels and increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, kidney problems, and eye damage.  

How blood pressure is measured  
• A cuff is placed around the upper arm and inflated.  
• The reading is given as two numbers, for example 130/80 mm Hg.  
 - The first (systolic) number shows the pressure when the heart beats and pushes blood out.  
 - The second (diastolic) number shows the pressure when the heart rests between beats.  

What counts as high  
• Normal: less than 120/80 mm Hg  
• Elevated: 120‑129 systolic and less than 80 diastolic  
• Hypertension stage 1: 130‑139 systolic or 80‑89 diastolic  
• Hypertension stage 2: 140 or higher systolic or 90 or higher diastolic  

Common causes and risk factors  
• Age – blood vessels become stiffer as we get older.  
• Family history – the condition can run in families.  
• Being overweight or obese.  
• Too much salt (sodium) in the diet.  
• Lack of physical activity.  
• Smoking and excessive alcohol use.  
• Certain medical conditions such as kidney disease or hormonal disorders.  

How it’s managed  
• Lifestyle changes: eating a balanced diet low in salt, staying active, maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol, and quitting smoking.  
• Medications: doctors may prescribe pills that help relax blood vessels, reduce fluid volume, or lower heart rate.  

Regular check‑ups are important because hypertension often has no symptoms, so you might not know you have it until a doctor measures your blood pressure. Keeping the numbers in a healthy range helps protect your heart and overall health.

Irritable bowel syndrome, often called IBS, is a common condition that affects the way the large intestine (the part of the gut that stores waste) works. It does not cause damage to the intestine, but it can cause uncomfortable symptoms that come and go.

**What happens in IBS?**  
The muscles in the wall of the colon may contract too strongly or too weakly. This irregular movement can make food move through the gut too quickly or too slowly, leading to the symptoms people notice.

**Typical symptoms**

• Cramping or pain in the belly, often relieved after a bowel movement  
• Diarrhea (loose, watery stools) or constipation (hard, difficult-to-pass stools), sometimes alternating between the two  
• A feeling that the bowels are not completely empty after a bathroom visit  
• Bloating or a sensation of gas building up in the abdomen  

**What can make symptoms worse?**  

• Certain foods (for example, fatty foods, caffeine, alcohol, or foods that cause gas)  
• Stress or strong emotions  
• Hormonal changes, such as those that occur during a menstrual period  

**How is IBS diagnosed?**  
Doctors usually diagnose IBS by asking about symptoms, medical history, and sometimes doing simple tests to rule out other conditions. There is no single test that confirms IBS.

**Ways to manage IBS**

• **Diet changes** – keeping a food diary can help identify trigger foods; some people find relief by following a low‑FODMAP diet (a plan that limits certain short‑chain carbs that can ferment in the gut).  
• **Regular meals** – eating at consistent times and not skipping meals can help regulate bowel movements.  
• **Fiber** – soluble fiber (found in oats, apples, and carrots) can help with both diarrhea and constipation, but too much insoluble fiber (found in whole‑grain breads and nuts) may worsen symptoms for some people.  
• **Stress reduction** – techniques such as deep breathing, meditation, yoga, or counseling can lower the impact of stress on the gut.  
• **Medications** – depending on the dominant symptom, doctors may suggest over‑the‑counter remedies (like anti‑diarrheal agents or laxatives) or prescription medicines that target gut muscle activity or pain.  

**When to see a doctor**  
If you notice blood in your stool, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, or symptoms that are getting worse, it’s important to get medical attention. These signs could point to a different condition that needs specific treatment.

In short, IBS is a functional disorder of the gut that causes pain, changes in stool consistency, and bloating. While it can be uncomfortable, many people find relief by adjusting their diet, managing stress, and using appropriate treatments under a doctor’s guidance.

Kidney stones form when substances that are normally dissolved in urine become too concentrated and start to stick together. Several factors can make this happen:

• **Not drinking enough fluids** – When you’re dehydrated, urine is more concentrated, giving crystals a better chance to grow.

• **Dietary habits** – Eating a lot of foods high in salt, animal protein (like meat, eggs, and fish), or oxalate (found in spinach, nuts, chocolate, and tea) can increase the amount of stone‑forming chemicals in the urine.

• **Certain medical conditions** – Some illnesses, such as gout, inflammatory bowel disease, or infections of the urinary tract, change the chemistry of urine and promote stone formation.

• **Family history and genetics** – If close relatives have had kidney stones, you may be more likely to develop them because of inherited traits that affect how your body handles minerals.

• **Medications and supplements** – Some drugs (for example, certain diuretics or calcium‑based antacids) and high‑dose vitamin C or D supplements can raise the levels of stone‑forming substances.

• **Metabolic problems** – Conditions that cause the body to excrete too much calcium, uric acid, cystine, or other substances can lead to stones.

In short, kidney stones develop when urine becomes too saturated with minerals or other compounds, and the body doesn’t have enough water or the right balance of chemicals to keep them dissolved. Staying well‑hydrated, eating a balanced diet, and managing any underlying health issues can help lower the risk.

Polycystic ovary syndrome, often called PCOS, is a common health condition that affects how a woman’s ovaries work. The ovaries are the organs that release eggs each month and make hormones such as estrogen and progesterone. In PCOS the ovaries may have many small, harmless cysts (tiny fluid‑filled sacs) and they often produce more male‑type hormones (androgens) than usual. This hormonal imbalance can change the way the menstrual cycle works and cause other symptoms.

**Key points about PCOS**

• **Hormone imbalance** – higher levels of androgens (male‑type hormones) can lead to acne, excess facial or body hair, and thinning hair on the scalp.  
• **Irregular periods** – periods may be infrequent, very heavy, or stop altogether because the ovaries do not release eggs regularly.  
• **Polycystic ovaries** – an ultrasound may show many small cysts on the ovaries, but the presence of cysts alone does not define PCOS.  
• **Weight changes** – many people with PCOS gain weight easily, especially around the belly, and may find it harder to lose weight.  
• **Fertility challenges** – because ovulation (the release of an egg) is irregular, getting pregnant can be more difficult.  
• **Metabolic effects** – PCOS can raise the risk of insulin resistance (the body’s cells don’t respond well to insulin), which can lead to higher blood sugar, pre‑diabetes, or type 2 diabetes, and increase the chance of high blood pressure and cholesterol problems.

**What may cause PCOS?**  
The exact cause is not known, but several factors are thought to play a role:

• Genetics – it often runs in families, so inherited traits may be involved.  
• Hormone signals – the brain’s pituitary gland may send stronger signals to the ovaries, causing them to make extra androgens.  
• Insulin resistance – high insulin levels can stimulate the ovaries to produce more androgens.

**How is PCOS diagnosed?**  
Doctors usually look at three things and need at least two of them to make a diagnosis:

1. Irregular or absent menstrual periods.  
2. Signs of excess androgen (such as acne, excess hair growth, or hair thinning).  
3. Ultrasound showing many small follicles (cysts) on the ovaries.

Blood tests may be done to check hormone levels and to look for insulin resistance or other health issues.

**Treatment and management**

There is no cure, but many options help control symptoms and lower health risks:

• **Lifestyle changes** – a balanced diet, regular physical activity, and weight management can improve insulin sensitivity and help regulate periods.  
• **Birth control pills** – combined oral contraceptives can make periods more regular and lower androgen levels, helping with acne and unwanted hair growth.  
• **Medications for insulin resistance** – drugs such as metformin can improve how the body uses insulin and may help restore regular cycles.  
• **Fertility treatments** – if pregnancy is desired, doctors may prescribe medications that stimulate ovulation, such as clomiphene or letrozole.  
• **Hair‑removal methods** – laser, electrolysis, or topical creams can reduce excess hair growth if it is bothersome.  
• **Skin care** – topical or oral acne treatments can be used for breakouts.

**Living with PCOS**

• Keep regular appointments with a healthcare provider to monitor blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood‑sugar levels.  
• Track menstrual cycles and any changes in symptoms; this information helps guide treatment.  
• Seek support from groups or counselors, as PCOS can affect mood and self‑image.

Overall, PCOS is a hormonal condition that can affect many aspects of health, but with proper care and lifestyle choices most people can manage symptoms and reduce long‑term risks.

Anemia is a condition where the blood does not have enough healthy red blood cells or enough hemoglobin, the part of the cell that carries oxygen. When there isn’t enough oxygen‑rich blood, you may feel tired, weak, short of breath, or notice that your skin looks paler than usual.

**Main reasons anemia can develop**

• **Blood loss** – Losing blood reduces the number of red cells. This can happen from:
  – Heavy menstrual periods
  – Surgery or injury that causes bleeding
  – Stomach ulcers, hemorrhoids, or other sources of hidden bleeding

• **Not enough red‑cell production** – The bone marrow (the spongy tissue inside bones that makes blood cells) may not make enough red cells because of:
  – Iron deficiency (iron is a mineral needed to build hemoglobin)
  – Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (these vitamins help the body form new red cells)
  – Certain chronic illnesses that affect the marrow, such as kidney disease or cancer
  – Exposure to chemicals or radiation that damage the marrow

• **Red‑cell destruction that is too fast** – Sometimes red cells break down sooner than they should, a process called hemolysis. Causes include:
  – Autoimmune diseases where the body attacks its own cells
  – Infections like malaria
  – Certain inherited conditions (for example, sickle‑cell disease or thalassemia) that make cells fragile

• **Chronic diseases** – Long‑standing illnesses such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, or chronic kidney disease can interfere with red‑cell production, leading to what doctors call “anemia of chronic disease.”

• **Inherited (genetic) disorders** – Some people are born with genes that affect how hemoglobin or red cells are made. Examples are:
  – Sickle‑cell disease (abnormal hemoglobin that makes cells break apart)
  – Thalassemia (reduced production of normal hemoglobin)

• **Other factors** – Poor nutrition, alcoholism, certain medications, and pregnancy (which increases the body’s need for iron and other nutrients) can also contribute to anemia.

In short, anemia can result from losing blood, not making enough new red cells, losing cells too quickly, or having other health problems that interfere with the normal balance of red‑cell production and destruction. If you suspect you have anemia, a doctor can run simple blood tests to find out the cause and recommend the right treatment.

Yes. Smoking is one of the strongest known causes of lung cancer.

Why smoking raises the risk  
• Tobacco smoke contains many chemicals that can damage the DNA inside cells. DNA is the set of instructions that tells cells how to grow and divide. When DNA is damaged, cells can start to grow out of control, which is what cancer is.  
• The more cigarettes a person smokes and the longer they have smoked, the higher the chance that enough damage will build up to cause cancer. This is called a “dose‑response” relationship.  
• Even people who quit smoking still have a higher risk than never‑smokers, but the risk drops steadily after quitting. After about 10–15 years without smoking, the risk becomes much closer to that of someone who never smoked.  

How big is the increase?  
• About 85‑90 % of all lung‑cancer cases in the United States are linked to smoking.  
• A lifelong smoker (for example, someone who has smoked a pack a day for 30 years) is roughly 20 times more likely to develop lung cancer than a person who has never smoked.  

Other ways smoke can affect you  
• Breathing in secondhand smoke (the smoke that comes from someone else’s cigarette) also raises the risk of lung cancer, though the increase is smaller than for a smoker.  
• Smoking also raises the risk of many other cancers (such as throat, mouth, bladder, and pancreas) and many non‑cancer diseases like heart disease and chronic lung disease.  

What can be done?  
• The most effective step is to stop smoking. Quitting at any age improves health and lowers cancer risk.  
• If you find it hard to quit, ask a health professional about counseling, nicotine‑replacement products, or prescription medicines that can help.  

In short, smoking dramatically increases the chance of getting lung cancer, but quitting can greatly reduce that risk over time.

Aspirin is often used after a heart attack to help keep another one from happening. This is called “secondary prevention” – using a treatment to stop a repeat problem in someone who has already had it.

Why aspirin can help  

• Aspirin makes platelets (tiny blood cells that help clotting) less sticky.  
• When platelets are less sticky, blood clots are less likely to form in the arteries that supply the heart.  
• Most heart attacks are caused by a clot that blocks a coronary artery, so reducing clot formation can lower the chance of another attack.

What the research shows  

• Large studies have compared people who take a low‑dose aspirin after a heart attack with people who do not.  
• The studies consistently found that low‑dose aspirin (usually 75–100 mg a day) reduces the risk of a second heart attack by about 15‑25 percent.  
• Aspirin also lowers the risk of death from heart disease and of having a stroke in many patients.

When aspirin may not be right  

• Aspirin can increase bleeding, especially in the stomach or brain.  
• People with a history of serious stomach ulcers, bleeding disorders, or certain allergies may be advised not to take it.  
• Doctors may adjust the dose or choose a different medicine if the bleeding risk is high.

How it is usually used  

• The dose for secondary prevention is low – often one “baby” aspirin (81 mg) or a regular low‑dose tablet (75 mg).  
• It is taken once a day, usually with food to lessen stomach irritation.  
• The decision to start or continue aspirin should be made together with a health‑care provider, who will weigh the heart‑protective benefit against any bleeding risk.

Key points to remember  

• For most people who have already had a heart attack, daily low‑dose aspirin does lower the chance of another attack.  
• The benefit is strongest when the medication is taken as prescribed and combined with other heart‑healthy measures (healthy diet, regular activity, blood‑pressure control, cholesterol‑lowering drugs, quitting smoking).  
• Always discuss with your doctor before starting, stopping, or changing the dose of aspirin, because individual health factors determine whether it is the best choice for you.

Yes. Being overweight or obese makes it more likely that a person will develop knee osteoarthritis, and it can also make the condition worse.

Why extra weight matters  

• **More load on the joint** – The knee has to support the weight of the whole body. Every extra pound adds about four pounds of pressure on each knee when you stand, and even more when you walk or climb stairs. This extra pressure speeds up the wear and tear of the cartilage, the smooth tissue that cushions the ends of the bones.  

• **Inflammation** – Fat tissue releases chemicals called cytokines that can cause low‑grade inflammation throughout the body. This inflammation can affect the knee joint and contribute to the breakdown of cartilage.  

• **Changes in movement** – Carrying extra weight can alter the way you walk or stand, putting uneven stress on parts of the knee and increasing the risk of damage.

How strong is the link?  

• Studies show that people with a body‑mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m² or higher (the usual definition of obesity) have about twice the risk of developing knee osteoarthritis compared with people of normal weight.  

• The risk rises even more as BMI increases. For each 5‑unit rise in BMI, the chance of knee osteoarthritis goes up by roughly 30‑40 percent.  

• The relationship is strongest for the knee; obesity is a weaker risk factor for osteoarthritis in the hip or hand.

What can be done?  

• **Weight loss** – Losing even 5–10 % of body weight can reduce the load on the knees and lower pain. For example, dropping 10 pounds can cut the pressure on each knee by about 40 pounds.  

• **Exercise** – Low‑impact activities such as walking, swimming, or cycling help strengthen the muscles around the knee, improve joint stability, and support weight loss.  

• **Healthy diet** – Eating a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein can aid weight control and provide nutrients that support joint health.

In short, obesity is a clear and modifiable risk factor for knee osteoarthritis. Managing weight through diet and safe exercise can lower the chance of developing the condition and can also lessen symptoms if osteoarthritis is already present.

Yes. Infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori (often called H. pylori) is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease.

**Why the link exists**

• H. pylori lives in the lining of the stomach and the upper part of the small intestine.  
• It produces substances that damage the protective mucus layer, allowing stomach acid to irritate the underlying tissue.  
• The ongoing irritation can create a sore, or ulcer, in the stomach lining (gastric ulcer) or in the first part of the small intestine (duodenal ulcer).  

**How common is the connection?**

• About 70‑90 % of people with duodenal ulcers have H. pylori infection.  
• Around 50‑70 % of people with gastric ulcers are infected with the bacterium.  
• Conversely, many people carry H. pylori without ever developing an ulcer, but the infection greatly raises the risk.

**What this means for treatment**

• If an ulcer is found, doctors usually test for H. pylori (breath test, stool test, blood test, or a biopsy during endoscopy).  
• When the infection is present, treatment combines antibiotics (to kill the bacteria) with medicines that reduce stomach acid.  
• Eradicating H. pylori heals most ulcers and lowers the chance they will come back.

**Bottom line**

H. pylori infection is strongly associated with peptic ulcer disease. Detecting and treating the infection is a key part of managing and preventing ulcers.

Yes. The human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine has been shown to lower the number of women who develop cervical precancer.

What cervical precancer means  
• The cervix is the lower part of the uterus.  
• Precancerous changes are called “CIN” (cervical intra‑epithelial neoplasia).  
• CIN is graded 1, 2 or 3; grades 2 and 3 (CIN2/3) are the lesions that most often turn into cancer if they are not treated.

How the vaccine works  
• The vaccine protects against the HPV types that cause most cervical cancer, especially types 16 and 18, and in newer versions also types 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58.
